blocks.content: docker restart is exactly what it sounds like: stop, then start, the same container, in one command.

There is nothing new happening under the hood, docker restart runs the same graceful stop sequence (SIGTERM, grace period, SIGKILL fallback) covered in docker stop, then immediately starts the container again, exactly like docker start.

blocks.alt: Stop, then immediately start again, in one command

blocks.content:
docker restart web
# Equivalent to: docker stop web && docker start web

code.content:
docker restart web
# Equivalent to: docker stop web && docker start web

codes.bash:
docker restart web
# Equivalent to: docker stop web && docker start web

blocks.content: 2. When You Actually Reach for This
blocks.text: 2. When You Actually Reach for This

blocks.content: A common real trigger is a configuration or environment change that a running process needs to reload, restarting is often the simplest way to make a container pick up new environment variables or a mounted config file without touching the image or recreating anything.

blocks.alt: Restarting is a quick way to force a config reload

blocks.content: 3. Restart vs Recreate: a Real Distinction
blocks.text: 3. Restart vs Recreate: a Real Distinction

blocks.content: It matters that restart keeps the same container ID and writable layer, while removing and re-running a container (docker rm followed by docker run) creates a genuinely new one, with a fresh writable layer and a new ID. Use restart when you want the same container back, use recreate when you actually want a clean slate, most commonly after changing the image itself.

blocks.alt: Restart keeps identity, recreate starts clean

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker restart is stop followed by start on the same container, useful for forcing a config reload without touching the image.
If you need a genuinely fresh writable layer, or you changed the image, remove and re-run instead of restarting.
